title: How to do squats for SIZE
summary: NH's method for squatting for leg size: pick the squat style that suits your build (high bar, low bar or front), find a medium-to-close stance, and rotate knee-flexion variations instead of spamming one squat. He treats depth as something to build gradually but cut short when it causes butt wink or pain, and manages lower-back fatigue so you can squat for years. He adds dead hangs and daily walking for spinal and general health.
claims: The squat is the king of lower-body development; if you want big legs you should squat
Consciously pick your squat style (high bar, low bar or front) by what feels natural for your build, not by what looks good; years on an unsuited style are wasted
Low-bar squats look silly to some, but if they suit your build they are the right choice; nobody sees you squat, only your legs
The front squat is fine as a main lift but it is highly technical and takes heavy investment to learn
As a beginner, vary your main squat with paused squats to reinforce technique and add hypertrophy instead of exotic variations
Your stance will keep evolving for months or years; experiment with lighter weight to find it
For size, keep the squat a knee-flexion movement, not a hip hinge: very wide stances can raise your squat but reduce knee flexion and quad growth, so aim for medium to close
Once the main squat is mastered, add variations: hack squat, front squat, SSB squat; spamming one squat style is not the way
Novice programs that have you back squat three times a week with no variations are really powerlifting programs and lead to lower-back and knee injuries
What you want is knee-flexion volume with progression; carryover between knee-flexion variations is very high
His leg size came from back squats plus lots of SSB and front squats; when he only back squatted he regressed and got hurt
He high-bar squats only about every eight days so it stays exciting, while doing some knee flexion all the time
Rotating squat variations prevents boredom and overuse injuries, because slight changes in joint angle shift the strain while still training the same muscles
Minimalism is always limiting for lower body; branch out from one squat
More range of motion is not always better; deeper squats give more stretch, but if depth causes joint pain, cut it
Treat depth as part of progression: build it gradually like load, but stop where your anatomy limits you; ass-to-grass is impossible for some builds
The last few inches of depth add little hypertrophy; if they cause lost tightness, good-morning squats or injury, cut the range
Safety and repeatability beat a few inches of depth every time
Tall lifters with long femurs (around 6'4) are usually better off low-bar squatting to parallel
Butt wink is a power leak where the lumbar spine rolls under you; stop the rep just before it occurs
Most lower-back pain in the back squat comes from butt wink, and more lower-back injuries happen in the barbell back squat than in the deadlift
Range of motion is a variation tool: he back squats to parallel or slightly below and goes ass-to-grass on front squats, which spare the lower back
People get big legs from squatting weekly for years, not from six months of three-times-a-week novice programs
Upper back and legs are the two most underdeveloped areas in natural lifters; natural quads and hamstrings have enormous size potential
Barbell back squats carry heavy axial loading; the spine is made to be loaded but can be overused, so be conservative
Squats and deadlifts share one lower back, so fatigue management is essential if you program both hip hinges and knee flexions
He does heavy hip hinges and knee flexions every two days, made possible by strategies that reduce lower-back fatigue
Use unilateral movements, leg press or Smith machine squats to add leg volume without taxing the lower back, as many tall lifters do
He believes a person's health and integrity depend on keeping the ability to squat and hinge heavy, even if that means reducing volume and intensity
Training legs once a week makes big legs hard; his gentleman split alternates upper and lower to train legs every two days with 48 hours between sessions
The advice to do more back and hamstring volume than quad volume does not mean doubling hip hinges; do hinges with styles that reduce axial loading
The main reason people cannot squat for years is a spinal injury, so managing the spine is what produces big legs long-term
Dead hang from a bar after every squat and deadlift day to decompress the spine while also training grip, forearms and core
Walk and get steps daily; only squatting left him with sore feet and ankles and reduced walking ability
Cardio does not kill gains; poor conditioning limits how hard you can recruit your legs on squats
